'''bean-stalk''' (bēn′stâk), ''n.'' The stem of a bean, or the whole plant: as, Jack and the ''bean-stalk.''

'''bean-tree''' (bēn′trē), ''n.'' A name given to the ''Pyrus intermedia'' of northern Europe, and to species of ''Bauhinia;'' in Australia, to the Moreton Bay chestnut, ''Castanospermum Australe;'' in the United States, sometimes, to ''Catalpa bignonioides;'' and in Jamaica, to ''Erythrina Corallodendron.''

'''bean-trefoil''' (bēn′trē″foil), ''n.'' '''1.''' The laburnum, ''Cytisus Laburnum,'' a leguminous shrub with trifoliate leaves. See ''laburnum.''—'''2.''' The ''Anagyris fœtida,'' a similar shrub of southern Europe, whose violet-colored seeds are said to be poisonous like those of the laburnum.—'''3.''' The buckbean, ''Menyanthes trifoliata.'' [Rare.]

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bean-stalk|489|bear}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''bean-stalk''' (bēn′stâk), ''n.'' The stem of a bean, or the whole plant: as, Jack and the ''bean-stalk.''

'''bean-tree''' (bēn′trē), ''n.'' A name given to the ''Pyrus intermedia'' of northern Europe, and to species of ''Bauhinia;'' in Australia, to the Moreton Bay chestnut, ''Castanospermum Australe;'' in the United States, sometimes, to ''Catalpa bignonioides;'' and in Jamaica, to ''Erythrina Corallodendron.''

'''bean-trefoil''' (bēn′trē″foil), ''n.'' '''1.''' The laburnum, ''Cytisus Laburnum,'' a leguminous shrub with trifoliate leaves. See ''laburnum.''—'''2.''' The ''Anagyris fœtida,'' a similar shrub of southern Europe, whose violet-colored seeds are said to be poisonous like those of the laburnum.—'''3.''' The buckbean, ''Menyanthes trifoliata.'' [Rare.]

'''bean-weevil''' (bēn′wē″vil), ''n.'' An American species of the genus ''Bruchus,'' which attacks {{img float|file=century v01 p0515 c1f1.png|width=235px|align=right|cap={{smaller|''a'', Bean-weevil (''Bruchus fabæ''). ''b'', Bean from which the beetles have issued. (Small figure shows natural size.)}}}} beans. {{smaller|It has been described as ''Bruchus fabæ'' (Riley), but is held by Horn to be identical with the ''B. obsoletus'' (Say). The species averages 3 millimeters in length, with the general color dark and piceous, the whole body being covered with rather dense cinereous pubescence, and the elytra being indistinctly mottled by transverse bands of darker pubescence. It infests stored beans, and there are usually several, sometimes as many as 15, specimens in a single bean.}}

'''beany''' (bē′ni), ''a.''   [< ''bean''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.]   In good condition (like a bean-fed horse); spirited; fresh. [Slang.] ''N. E. D.''

'''bear'''<sup>1</sup> (bãr), ''v.''; pret. ''bore'' (formerly, and still in the archaic style, ''bare''), pp. ''borne'', ''born'' (now only in a single sense: see note at end), ppr. ''bearing''.   [< ME. ''beren'' (pret. ''bar'', ''bare'', pl. ''bare'', ''bere'', ''beren'', pp. ''boren'', rarely ''born''), < AS. ''beran'' (pret. ''bær'', pl. ''bǣron'', pp. ''boren'') = OS. ''beran'' = OFries. ''bera'' = D. ''baren'' = OHG. ''beran'' = Icel. ''bera'' = Sw. ''bära'' = Dan. ''bære'' = Goth. ''bairan'', bear (also in comp. OS. ''giberan'' = AS. ''geberan'' = OHG. ''geberen'', MHG. ''gebern'', G. ''gebären'' = Goth. ''gabairan'', bear, in MHG. and G. bring forth), = L. ''ferre'' = Gr. φέρειν = Skt. √ ''bhar'', bear, carry. A very prolific root in all the languages, both in form and senses. From the AS. come ''barrow''<sup>2</sup>, ''bier'', ''barm''<sup>1</sup>, ''barn''<sup>2</sup>, ''bairn'', ''birth''<sup>1</sup>, ''burthen''<sup>1</sup>, ''burden''<sup>1</sup>, etc.; from the L. ''fertile'', ''confer'', ''defer'', ''differ'', ''infer'', etc., ''Lucifer'', ''conifer'', etc., ''auriferous'', ''vociferous'', etc., and other words in ''-fer'', ''-ferous''; from the Gr. ''semaphore'', ''hydrophore'', ''phosphorous'', ''electrophorus'', etc., and other words in ''-phore'', ''-phorous'', etc.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To support; hold up; sustain: as, a pillar or a girder ''bears'' the superincumbent weight.
{{smaller block|<poem>Sage he stood,
With Atlantean shoulders fit to ''bear''
The weight of mightiest monarchies.</poem>{{right|''Milton'', P. L., ii. 306.}}}}
'''2.''' To support in movement; carry; convey.
{{smaller block|Whither do these ''bear'' the ephah? {{right|Zech. v. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>From the unshaken rock the torrent hoarse
''Bears'' off its broken waves, and seeks a devious course.</poem> {{right|''Scott'', Vision of Don Roderick, Conclusion, st. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And down a rocky pathway from the place
There came a fair-hair’d youth, that in his hand
''Bare'' victual for the mowers.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}
'''3.''' To suffer; endure; undergo: as, to ''bear'' punishment, blame, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>Alas, how many ''bear'' such shameful blows,
Which not themselves but he that gives them knows!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 832.}}}}
'''4.''' To endure the effects of; take the consequences of; be answerable for.
{{smaller block|He shall ''bear'' their iniquities.
{{right|Isa. liii. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Sir, let her ''bear'' her sins on her own head;
Vex not yourself.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', King and No King, i. 1.}}}}
'''5.''' To support or sustain without sinking, yielding, shrinking, or suffering injury.
{{smaller block|A wounded spirit who can ''bear?''
{{right|Prov. xviii. 14.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Console if you will, I can ''bear'' it;
’Tis a well-meant alms of breath.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', After the Burial.}}}}
{{smaller block|Anger and jealousy can no more ''bear'' to lose sight of their objects than love.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, i. 10.}}}}
'''6.''' To suffer or sustain without violence, injury, or change; admit or be capable of.
{{smaller block|In all criminal cases the most favourable interpretation should be put on words that they can possibly ''bear.''
{{right|''Swift.''}}}}
{{smaller block|The motives of the best actions will not ''bear'' too strict an inquiry.
{{right|''Swift'', Thoughts on Various Subjects.}}}}

'''7.''' To suffer without resentment or effort to prevent; endure patiently.
{{smaller block|It was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have ''borne'' it.
{{right|Ps. lv. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>With your long-practis’d patience ''bear'' afflictions.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Spanish Curate, i. 2.}}}}

'''8.''' To sustain, as expense; supply the means of paying.
{{smaller block|Somewhat that will ''bear'' your charges.
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}

'''9.''' To have, or have a right to; be entitled to; have the rightful use of, as a name, a title, a coat of arms, and the like.
{{smaller block|We are no enemies to what are commonly called conceits, but authors ''bear'' them, as heralds say, with a difference.
{{right|''Lowell'', Study Windows, p. 336.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Who in the Lord God’s likeness ''bears'' the keys
To bind or loose.</poem>
{{right|''Swinburne'', Laus Veneris.}}}}

'''10.''' To carry, as in show; exhibit; show.
{{smaller block|''Bear'' welcome in your eye.
{{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, i. 5.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Which, like a waxen image ’gainst a fire,
''Bears'' no impression of the thing it was.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., ii. 4.}}}}

'''11.''' To bring forward; render; give; afford: as, to ''bear'' testimony.
{{smaller block|Thou shalt not ''bear'' false witness against thy neighbour.
{{right|Ex. xx. 16.}}}}

'''12.''' To carry in the mind; entertain or cherish, as love, hatred, envy, respect, etc.
{{smaller block|<poem>If I can catch him once upon the hip,
I will feed fat the ancient grudge I ''bear'' him.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The reverent care I ''bear'' unto my lord
Made me collect these dangers in the duke.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The great and guilty love he ''bare'' the queen.</poem> {{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}}
'''13.''' To possess, as a property, attribute, or characteristic; have in or on; contain: as, to ''bear'' signs or traces; to ''bear'' an inscription; the contents which the letter ''bears.''
{{smaller block|<poem>What, think you much to pay two thousand crowns,
And ''bear'' the name and port of gentleman?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iv. 1.}}}}
'''14.''' To possess and use, as power; exercise; be charged with; administer: as, to ''bear'' sway.
{{smaller block|Here’s another letter to her: she ''bears'' the purse too; she is a region in Guiana, all gold and bounty.
{{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., i. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|Russia soon showed that she was resolved to ''bear'' a part in the quarrels as well as the negotiations of her neighbours. {{right|''Brougham.''}}}}
'''15†.''' To carry on; deal with.
{{smaller block|This can be no trick: The conference was sadly ''borne.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, ii. 3.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Beware
Of entrance to a quarrel; but, being in,
''Bear'' ’t, that the opposed may beware of thee.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 3.}}}}
'''16.''' To manage; direct; use (what is under the immediate control of one’s will).
{{smaller block|<poem>''Bear'' your body more seeming.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, v. 4.}}}}
Hence, with a reflexive pronoun, to behave; act in any character: as, he ''bore himself'' nobly. —'''17.''' To sustain by vital connection; put forth as an outgrowth or product; produce by natural growth: as, plants ''bear'' leaves, flowers, and fruit; the heroes ''borne'' by ancient Greece.
{{smaller block|Can the fig-tree . . . ''bear'' olive-berries? {{right|Jas. iii. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Here dwelt the man divine whom Samos ''bore.''</poem>
{{right|''Dryden.''}}}}
<poem>Life that ''bears'' immortal fruit.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, xl.}}}}

'''18.''' To bring forth in parturition; give birth to, as young; figuratively, give rise or origin to. [The past participle ''born'' is now used only in this sense. See remarks below.]
{{smaller block|And she conceived, and ''bare'' Cain, and said, I have gotten a man from the Lord. {{right|Gen. iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|I can tell thee where that saying was ''born.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 5.}}}}

'''19.''' To conduct; guide; take: as, he ''bore'' him off to his quarters.
{{smaller block|''Bear'' me forthwith unto his creditor.
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., iv. 4.}}}}

'''20.''' To press; thrust; push; drive; urge: with some word to denote the direction in which the object is driven: as, to ''bear'' down a scale; to ''bear'' back the crowd.
{{smaller block|The residue were so disordered as they could not conveniently fight or fly, and not only justled and ''bore'' down one another, but, in their confused tumbling back, brake a part of the avant-guard. {{right|''Sir J. Hayward.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Confidence then ''bore'' thee on; secure
Either to meet no danger, or to find
Matter of glorious trial. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 1175.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|<poem>How the rushing waves
''Bear'' all before them.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', Flood of Years.}}}}

'''21.''' To gain or win: now commonly with ''away'' or ''off;'' formerly, sometimes, with an indefinite ''it'' for the object. {{smaller block|Some think to ''bear it'' by speaking a great word.
{{right|''Bacon'', Of Seeming Wise.}}}}
'''22.''' In the game of backgammon, to throw off or remove, as the men from the board.—'''23.''' To purport; imply; import; state.
{{smaller block|The letters ''bore'' that succour was at hand. {{right|''Scott.''}}}}
{{smaller|[''Bear'', signifying to bring forth, when used passively, especially as an adjective, has the past participle ''born'' (bôrn), but when used after the verb ''have'', or followed by ''by'', ''borne'' (bōrn), the latter having a more direct reference to the literal sense. Thus, a child was ''born;'' but, she has ''borne'' a child. In all the other senses both participles are spelled ''borne'': as, I have ''borne'' the expenses; the expenses must be ''borne''. The regular form, historically, is ''born'' (bōrn), like ''torn'', ''sworn''. The distinction is artificial and recent (after the middle of the eighteenth century).]—'''To bear a hand,''' to lend a hand quickly; take hold; give aid or assistance. [Naut. and colloq.]}}
{{smaller block|All hands ahoy! ''bear a hand'' and make sail.
{{right|''R. H. Dana, Jr.'', Before the Mast, p. 69.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To bear arms.''' See ''arm''<sup>2</sup>.—'''To bear away the bell.''' See ''bell''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To bear''' (a person) '''company.''' See ''company''.—'''To bear date,''' to have the mark of time when written or executed: as, the letter ''bears date'' Sept. 30, 1887.}}
{{smaller block|A public letter which ''bears date'' just a month after the admission of Francis Bacon [to Trinity College].
{{right|''Macaulay'', Lord Bacon.}}}}
{{smaller|'''To bear down,''' to force down; figuratively, to overcome; vanquish: as, to ''bear down'' all opposition.—'''To bear in,''' in ''coal-mining'', to hole, undercut, or kirve. See ''hole'', ''v. t.'' [Pennsylvania anthracite region.]—'''To bear in hand†,''' to keep in hope or expectation; amuse with false pretenses; deceive.}}
{{smaller block|A rascally yea-forsooth knave! to ''bear'' a gentleman ''in hand'', and then stand upon security!
{{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., i. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Still ''bearing'' them ''in hand'',
Letting the cherry knock against their lips,</poem>}}
{{smaller block|And draw it by their mouths, and back again.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, i. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|What I take from her, I spend upon other wenches; ''bear'' her ''in hand'' still: she has wit enough to rob her husband, and I ways enough to consume the money.
{{right|''Middleton and Dekker'', Roaring Girl, ii. 1.}}}}

'''To bear in mind''', to keep in remembrance; have fixed in the memory.

{{smaller block|With reference to the effects of intercrossing and of competition, it should be ''borne in mind'' that most animals and plants keep to their proper homes, and do not needlessly wander about. {{right|''Darwin'', Origin of Species, p. 94.}}}}

'''To bear off.''' (''a''†) To sustain; endure.

{{smaller block|Do you suppose the state of this realm to be now so feeble that it cannot ''bear off'' a greater blow than this?
{{right|''Sir J. Hayward''.}}}}

(''b'') ''Naut.'', to remove to a distance; keep clear from rubbing against anything: as, to ''bear off'' a boat. (''c'') To gain and carry off: as, he ''bore off'' the prize.—'''To bear one hard'''†, to cherish a grudge toward a person.

<poem>Though he ''bear me hard'',
I yet must do him right. {{right|''B. Jonson''.}}</poem>

'''To bear out.''' (''a'') To give support or countenance to.

{{smaller block|Company only can ''bear'' a man ''out'' in an ill thing. {{right|''South''.}}}}

(''b'') To defend; support; uphold; second: with a personal object.

{{smaller block|If I cannot once or twice in a quarter ''bear out'' a knave against an honest man, I have but a very little credit with your worship. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., v. 1.}}}}

{{smaller block|I never suspected him to be a man of resolution or courage sufficient to ''bear'' him ''out'' in so desperate an attempt. {{right|''Swift'', Change in Queen’s Ministry.}}}}

{{smaller block|Æschines by no means ''bears'' him ''out''; and Plutarch directly contradicts him.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Mitford’s Hist. of Greece.}}}}

(''c'') To confirm; corroborate; establish; justify: with a thing for the object.

{{smaller block|That such oscillations [of climate] occurred during the Tertiary period seems to be ''borne out'' by the facts of geology and palæontology.
{{right|''J. Croll'', Climate and Cosmology, p. 160.}}}}

(''d''†) With a more or less indefinite ''it'' for the object: (1) To last through; endure.

<poem>Love alters not with his [Time’s] brief hours and weeks,
But ''bears it out'' even to the edge of doom.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, cxvi.}}}}
<poem>If that the Turkish fleet
Be not enshelter’d and embay’d, they are drown’d;
It is impossible to ''bear it out.''   ''Shak.'', Othello, ii. 1.</poem>

(2) To enable to endure; render supportable.

{{smaller block|Many a good hanging prevents a bad marriage; and for turning away, let summer ''bear it out.''
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 5.}}}}

'''To bear the bag.''' See ''bag''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To bear the bell.''' See ''bell''<sup>1</sup>.—'''To bear the gree.''' See ''gree''<sup>2</sup>.—'''To bear through'''†. (''a'') To run through with a sword or rapier. (''b'') To conduct or manage.

<poem>My hope is,
So to ''bear through'', and out, the consulship,
As spight shall ne’er wound you, though it may me.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''B. Jonson'', Catiline, iii. 1.}}}}

'''To bear up.''' (''a'') To support; keep from sinking.

{{smaller block|A religious hope does not only ''bear up'' the mind under her sufferings, but makes her rejoice in them.
{{right|''Addison.''}}}}

(''b''†) To arrange; contrive; devise.

<poem>''Isab.'' I have made him know
I have a servant comes with me along,
That stays upon me, whose persuasion is
I come about my brother.
''Duke.'' ’Tis well ''borne up.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', M. for M., iv. 1.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be capable of supporting or carrying: as, the floor would not ''bear.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
